thread.title: Nick's Picks 2018 Review: Undefeated Against The Market

author: Nicholas Ward
title: Nick's Picks 2018 Review: Undefeated Against The Market
text:
I absolutely hate it when I hear people say that investors (especially the every day, mom and pop, Main Street type of average Joe) cannot beat the market. Or, I suppose I should say, reliably beat the market over a long period of time.
It’s this sort of defeatist attitude that leads towards underperformance, I think. It’s this sort of pessimism that holds people down. I believe that this negative outlook is perpetuated by the money manager types and fund managers who rely on investors paying them fees for their business to work.
When I think about the amount of money thrown away by retail investors to money managers, I get sick to my stomach.
Granted, I had a bad relationship with a financial manager earlier in my life that may have tainted my perception of the profession. I’m sure that there are good people who genuinely want to see their clients succeed and meet their financial goals. Regardless, I think it’s a crying shame that so many retail investors believe that they are destined for average (or even below average) performance if they take hold of the reins of their own financial freedom.
With this in mind, I set out several years ago to prove that not only can retail investors beat the market over the long term, but they can do it with relatively little time or effort. This was how the Nick’s Picks series was born.
No, this isn’t a get rich scheme or anything like that. I don’t believe those exist. But I do believe that following a fairly simple strategy of owning high quality names and not falling victim to irrational emotions can result in outstanding returns. I simply wanted to show that the stock picking isn’t just for Wall Street wizards. It can be for people like you and me. People with no formal financial education, but instead, sheer gumption and common sense.
It doesn’t get much simpler than buying stock when the year starts, holding it until the end of the year, and then doing the whole thing all over again the next year, does it? That’s what Nick’s Picks is all about.
At the beginning on 2016, I gave myself a theoretical $100,000.00 to “invest” in this project portfolio using these rules. I pick any stock, ETF, fund, bond, asset, etc., I want on January first and hold it until the end of the year. Then, throughout the year, there are no trades. All dividends received throughout the year are pooled and added to the cash pile at the end of the year.
In almost every situation, I would recommend re-investing dividends for retail investors, but for the sake of simplicity within the Nick’s Picks portfolio project, I’ve decided to simply collect them and re-deploy them at the start of the next year.
Honestly, I don’t even look at the stocks all year (because I’m busy managing my personal portfolio). It’s fun, because most of the time by December I’ve forgotten some of what I picked in January and it’s a big surprise as I calculate the results to see how well I did.
And thankfully (for the sake of this experiment, which is meant to prove that anyone can beat the market), the results have been great. I’ve beaten the market every year since I started this project.
Here’s the recap article I wrote in 2016. That year, the S&P 500 posted 13.9% gains and Nick’s Picks posted gains of 16.5%.
Here’s the recap piece I wrote in 2017. That year, the S&P 500 was up 22.16% and Nick’s Picks posted gains of 22.90%.
For those of you who missed the original 2018 Nick's Picks piece, here's the link .
In 2018, the S&P 500 was down 6.23% and Nick’s Picks posted losses of just 2.19%. When you factor in dividends, the S&P 500 was down roughly 4.5% and Nick’s Picks almost turned positive, losing just 0.79%.
This cumulative performance means that the original $100,000.00 that I gave myself to “invest” with in 2016 has grown to $142,045.39 over the last 3 years. Had I invested that same theoretical money into the SPY, it would have grown to ~$132,900.00 over that same period of time.
I'll address this now because I'm sure it will come up in the comment section somewhere, but I used theoretical money for this portfolio rather than real dollars because I manage my personal portfolio much differently. I pay attention to the market day in and day out and make many trades throughout the year. I've done great with that strategy for myself, but that's not what Nick's Picks is all about.
I don't expect the average mom and pop investor to spend nearly as much time watching over and thinking about the markets as I do. And, as you can see by the results of this project, apparently, you don't have to. Nick's Picks has achieved very satisfactory results without having to make trades, worry about rebalancing throughout the year, making risk adjustments, or paying attention to the day to day market headlines.
Obviously I’m not pleased about my first negative year for the Nick’s Picks portfolio, but I am pleased about the relative alpha to the S&P 500, which represented fairly wide outperformance.
So, here’s how the portfolio shaped up at the end of the year.

I was caught off guard by the Chinese stocks, which fell drastically during the year because of the trade war, which I totally underestimated. This trade war has sparked global growth concerns, which, alongside the more hawkish Fed, has led to fears of recession which also really hurt the big banks that I picked for 2018. Thankfully, both of these groups represented fairly small portions of the portfolio.
Anheuser-Busch cut its dividend during the year and posted terrible total return performance. Nvidia was caught up in the risk-off mindset like so many other semi-conductors and posted strong, double-digit losses as well. Other names related to high growth technology were mixed. Alphabet was fairly flat, posting minimal losses while Amazon posted strong gains. Salesforce continued to be a top performer for the portfolio, making me wish I owned it in real life (CRM is one of the few names in Nick’s Picks that I don’t actually own).
Apple has been a core holding of the Nick’s Picks portfolio since the start and that name's big fall at the end of the year really hurt the portfolio’s performance. If it wasn’t for the double-digit drop in Apple during the last couple months of the year, I would have been positive for 2018.
The same thing goes for Johnson and Johnson. JNJ has been a core holding of the portfolio as well and was really hurt by the asbestos related reports at the end of the year that sent investors running for the doors.
Thankfully, the final core position, Disney, did fairly well, posting gains during a down year. I found this interesting because some of the other entertainment names I included, such as AT&T and Comcast posted negative results that surprised me.
The other top performers were my healthcare picks, which were positive across the board. Some other classic DGI names, like Boeing, Cisco, and Nike.
Overall, I think 2018’s version of Nick’s Picks just goes to show that amassing a collection of high quality companies (many of which pay growing dividends) is a great way to invest. The strategy continues to post market beating results and hopefully that will continue into 2019.
2019 Nick’s Picks have already been made. The portfolio has been put together for the new year, and in the coming days, I will publish an article detailing the choices that I made this year. I hope you all enjoyed this piece (especially those who’ve been following this project since its inception). I look forward to continuing the crusade against those who assume that retail investors cannot beat the market. Heck, as it turns out, not only can they do so, but they can do so spending about an hour per year managing a portfolio.
